# 2026 Azerbaijan Grand Prix (Baku) — pre-race forecast

Round 15, Saturday 26 September 2026, 51 laps of the 6.003 km Baku City Circuit.
Weekend brought forward one day for Azerbaijan’s Day of Remembrance. Forecast is after qualifying and grid penalties, before the race.

## Grid (after penalties)

1 Russell (Mercedes) 1:42.526  
2 Leclerc (Ferrari) +0.837  
3 Piastri (McLaren) +0.838  
4 Hadjar (Red Bull) +0.974  
5 Norris (McLaren) +1.146  
6 Hamilton (Ferrari) +1.332  
7 Gasly (Alpine) +1.521  
8 Verstappen (Red Bull) +1.555 (Q3 not representative)  
9 Colapinto (Alpine)  
10 Bearman (Haas)  
11 Lawson (Racing Bulls)  
12 Albon (Williams)  
13 Ocon (Haas)  
14 Sainz (Williams, 5-place yellow-flag penalty; qualified 9th)  
15 Lindblad (Racing Bulls)  
16 Antonelli (Mercedes, Q1 crash, no Q2 time)  
17 Bortoleto (Audi)  
18 Hulkenberg (Audi)  
19 Bottas (Cadillac)  
20 Perez (Cadillac, 3-place impeding penalty)  
21 Alonso (Aston Martin, PU components, back of grid)  
22 Stroll (Aston Martin, PU components, back of grid)

Hadjar returns after missing NED/ITA/ESP with a wrist injury. Lawson is back at Racing Bulls.

## Championship (after Madrid)

Antonelli 292, Russell 211 (−81), Hamilton 191, Norris 186, Leclerc 167, Verstappen 145, Piastri 120. Mercedes 503 in constructors. Antonelli has eight wins; Russell two.

## Pace picture

Mercedes dominated Thursday (Russell FP1/FP2). Verstappen nicked FP3 by 0.099s. Qualifying then split: Russell produced a 0.837s pole — biggest 2026 Mercedes one-lap win — while Antonelli clipped the T1 inside wall in Q1.

F1-compiled long runs tell a different story than that pole lap:

| Team | Est. race gap |
| Mercedes | — |
| McLaren | +0.05s |
| Red Bull | +0.30s |
| Ferrari | +0.34s |
| Alpine | +0.99s |

Russell’s own Thursday comment was that race pace looked closely matched with McLaren and Red Bull. Leclerc’s P2 used tows; Ferrari still trails on the straight. Verstappen was down on power throughout qualifying (~0.5s to Hadjar, 11 km/h down the trap) plus a battery abort and Norris’s yellow. Hadjar’s P4 is genuine but he was cautious on a sore wrist and worried about Red Bull launches into a long T1.

## Race character

Dry, ~26°C air, track ~43°C, 0% rain. Wind calmer than Friday’s 65 km/h quali gusts (race gusts ~43 km/h). Pirelli C3 hard / C4 medium / C5 soft; one-stop favoured, all three compounds live, hard may be ignored. Pit windows wide. 2026 active aero and energy deployment should help passing on the 2.2 km straight relative to older Baku, but the castle section remains a wall.

Unlike Madrid, this is not a processional prior. Baku combines real main-straight passing with a high genuine SC rate (Pirelli’s historical SC figure here is very high; model uses ~76% at least one SC/red rather than 89%, to avoid Madrid-style overfit).

## Model

280k-race Monte Carlo:

- Grid after penalties, with Red Bull start losses (Hadjar, Verstappen) and a T1 pack-damage draw.
- Three interruption regimes: green (~24%), single SC/VSC pit lottery (~44%), multi-SC/red (~32%).
- 68% chance Verstappen’s power is restored overnight.
- Driver-specific mechanical and wall hazards. Extra DNS/mechanical DNF for Antonelli (FP1 hydraulic + fire-damaged PU change + Q1 crash rebuild) following the Madrid Hamilton miss. Elevated Aston–Honda and Cadillac DNF priors held.
- Most retirements are NC; a minority of late stoppages still classify.

Headline probabilities (classified P1 / podium / top 10 / retirement):

| Driver | P(win) | P(podium) | P(top 10) | P(retirement) |
| Russell | 42.8% | 67.1% | 86.5% | 12.1% |
| Piastri | 17.6% | 58.9% | 85.4% | 12.9% |
| Norris | 12.1% | 48.7% | 85.1% | 13.2% |
| Leclerc | 9.6% | 45.4% | 83.6% | 14.1% |
| Antonelli | 5.7% | 18.7% | 73.6% | 23.0% |
| Verstappen | 4.5% | 18.3% | 80.6% | 15.9% |
| Hamilton | 3.7% | 18.7% | 80.6% | 15.8% |
| Hadjar | 3.2% | 17.2% | 77.7% | 18.7% |

Expected classified finishers ≈ 18.2 of 22. P1–P10 almost always filled; P22 occupancy ~1.6%.

## Grid vs call

Material departures: Piastri and Norris over Leclerc (McLaren race pace vs Ferrari, 0.001s quali gap between PIA and LEC); Norris and Hamilton over Hadjar (Red Bull launches + rust); Verstappen over Gasly (true pace, if the PU is even partly healthy); Antonelli from 16th to ~8th (Mercedes delta on a passing straight, SC-dependent for more). Track position holds from Gasly/Colapinto through the Williams/Audi/Cadillac/Aston group, with only small Haas/Racing Bulls swaps.

Antonelli himself said this is harder to overtake than Monza. The call is a points-to-P6 recovery if the car lasts, not a 19th-to-first repeat.

# Forecast notes

Winners: ANT x8, RUS x2, NOR x2, HAM (BCN), LEC (GBR).

### Baku weekend facts (for post-race review)
Grid after penalties: RUS, LEC, PIA, HAD, NOR, HAM, GAS, VER, COL, BEA, LAW, ALB, OCO, SAI (+5 yellow), LIN, ANT (Q1 T1 crash), BOR, HUL, BOT, PER (+3 impeding), ALO (PU), STR (PU).
Russell pole 1:42.526 by 0.837s (biggest 2026 Mercedes quali margin). Piastri 0.001s behind Leclerc. Verstappen P8 after power deficit (~0.5s to Hadjar), battery abort, Norris yellow. Antonelli: FP1 hydraulic + fire-damaged PU change, then Q1 crash — rebuild DNF flag.
F1 long-run: MER 0, MCL +0.05, RBR +0.30, FER +0.34, ALP +0.99. Dry Saturday, track ~43°C, wind calmer than quali. One-stop C3/C4/C5. Pre-race call: RUS favourite ~43% win; McLarens the live threat; ANT points-if-finishes not a Monza repeat.

## Madrid (Rd 14) result vs forecast — what to keep vs discard

Result: ANT, VER, NOR, LEC, RUS, LAW, COL, PIA, LIN, HUL | OCO, GAS, BOR, TSU, ALB, BEA, ALO, BOT. NC: HAM (brakes, lap 6), STR (brakes after damage, lap 12), PER (water/PU, lap 31), SAI (collision damage, lap 43). 18 classified vs E≈18.6.

Keep: ANT 36.5% win / NOR 33.9% was the right coin-flip (market +125/+130). Win Brier 0.024, podium Brier 0.026. Midfield almost grid-locked (P9–P18 moved 0 to +2). Processional prior was correct. Stroll highest DNF (~32%) hit. Cadillac/Aston at the back hit. One-stop + hard-to-pass character hit.

Do not overfit: VSC stealing Norris’s win; HAM’s first DNF of the year; Piastri’s T1 wing; F3’s 19 red flags (F1 had one VSC, no SC, no red). Do not bump ANT’s base rate just because he won; do not treat pole as a curse.

## Reusable modeling lessons

### 1. Three interruption regimes, not two
Madrid model mixed (a) green Plackett–Luce and (b) multi-SC/red-flag chaos. The race was a third, more common, modern-F1 state: **a single VSC that is a pit-phase lottery without enabling on-track reordering**.

- Leader who has just passed pit entry cannot stop; P2/P3 can take a cheap stop and jump them. That decided ANT vs NOR. VER also boxed under VSC → P2.
- Cars that park in a runoff gap (Stroll) often produce a **VSC, not a full SC**. Support-series red-flag counts overstate F1 red-flag/SC probability on a new circuit.
- On a no-overtake track, one VSC is enough to decide the win and still leave the rest of the field processional. Chaos-regime mass that lets “best race car from P6” win needs a full SC/red, which did not occur (RUS stayed P5).

Action: add an explicit **single-neutralization pit-lottery** regime. On processional tracks, shave leader win probability toward P2 whenever pit loss is large. Do not let F2/F3 red-flag counts dominate F1 SC/red priors.

### 2. Starting compound × interruption timing is first-order
Early VSC helped cars that **wanted** to stop soon (medium/soft one-stop: ANT, VER, HUL, COL). It hurt hard-tyre long-stint cars (LEC, RUS, PIA, LAW, GAS, BOR) who needed a *late* SC/red.

- LEC led ~32 laps on hards waiting for a late SC/red; pitted lap 48 → P4 (would have been P4 on the other strategy too).
- RUS: hard start, VSC onto mediums, second stop to hard → still P5. Overtaking dead, strategy could not pass LEC.
- GAS/BOR hung out to the end; no late incident → out of points.

Action: do not give generic “climber” points mass from P12–P16 on a processional track unless an interruption is likely *and* timed for their compound. Split-strategy value is timing-dependent, not a free “chaos overlay”.

### 3. Overnight rebuilds and thermal street-circuit DNFs
HAM: FP3 wall at T22, rebuilt overnight, Q4, superb launch, then brake-pedal failure (first DNF of his season). Forecast used a generic ~11% front-runner retirement — same as NOR/VER — and paid for it in retirement/points Brier.

STR also brakes (after early damage) in heat. Bottas spent the race managing brake temps. PER water-pressure/PU. Track into the 50s °C, heavy braking, long straights, banking.

Action:
- After an FP crash/rebuild, bump **mechanical** DNF (brakes, cooling, hydraulics, floor), not only DNS. The car that starts is not a healthy car.
- On hot, heavy-braking street circuits, elevate **brake/cooling/PU thermal** DNF vs “wall hit” DNF. Driver “car killer” quotes overstated *full-course* chaos; they were closer to right on *component* stress.
- Do not apply a uniform ~10–12% DNF to every top-10 car. Rebuild, new PU, and thermal-street flags should differentiate.

Field DNF count was fine (4 vs ~3.4). The miss was **who** DNFed (a P4 Ferrari), not the total.

### 4. Pack-start damage is sticky when passing is dead
Processional Plackett–Luce perturbs order; it understates “broken wing/floor on lap 1 → finish several places down with almost no recovery”.

- PIA: P7, squeezed by RUS, broken endplate, only stop couldn’t fix it, P8. Biggest position log-loss. P(top 10) was fine; the **place distribution was too peaked** around P5–P7.
- TSU: Sainz T1 contact, damaged, P14.
- SAI: T1 lockup vs TSU, later hit ALO, retired with damage.
- STR: opening-lap damage then brakes.

Action: on no-overtake layouts, give P6–P12 a fatter left tail (damage → +3–6 places lost, or NC). Pit-lane starters (BEA) also have little climb without a full SC; P16 from PL is typical, not a points tail.

### 5. Grid still dominates the midfield on this circuit type
COL 9→7, LIN 10→9, HUL 11→10, OCO 13→11, GAS 14→12, BOR 12→13, TSU 15→14, ALB 16→15, ALO 17→17, BOT 19→18. HAM’s early DNF was the main +1 shuffle.

Keep a strong track-position model from ~P8 back. Alpine (Mercedes PU) and Racing Bulls are the real midfield; Audi/Haas next; Williams off the pace; Aston/Cadillac fighting not to be last. Q3 slots (COL, LIN) converting to points is the default if they finish.

GAS as “most likely climber from P14” was the main midfield over-credit. Without a late SC, P14 on a processional track stays ~P12–P14.

### 6. Quali gap of 0.01s: prefer the better race car / championship leader
ANT from P2 beat polesitter after a VSC, but also had genuine Mercedes race pace and FP lockout. NOR was fastest in the race until the VSC; both belong in the high-30s win range when the gap is 0.011s. Do not collapse them to 50/50 on pole alone, and do not treat the VSC outcome as evidence NOR was mis-ranked.

VER P3 is sticky on a processional track if he finishes (here P2 via VSC + HAM DNF). He still could not match ANT/NOR on pace — “best of the rest” remains the Red Bull base.

### 7. Friday compound reading vs Sunday
Pirelli: C2 hard was little-run on Friday and was the race tyre (stints >45 laps). Medium/soft grained but were usable. Teams that over-indexed Friday long runs, or assumed two-stop from graining, were wrong.

Action: on a new street circuit, treat Friday tyre conclusions as weak. High pit loss + no passing makes one-stop the default even if Friday said otherwise. Hard can be the race tyre without Friday evidence.

### 8. Constructor reliability priors (do not shrink yet)
- Aston–Honda: still DNF-prone (STR) and slow (ALO P17). High retirement, near-zero points until the package actually scores.
- Cadillac–Ferrari PU: PER water/PU DNF, BOT last classified, 0 points in 14 races. Keep high DNF, negligible points.
- Williams: no pace (ALB “best we could hope”: beat Astons + one Haas). Points only via chaos.
- Audi: HUL P10 via VSC pit-stop vs OCO. Midfield points are a pit-execution / compound-timing thing, not race-pace overtake.

## Circuit-type flags for later rounds

- **No-overtake street / short T1 run** (Madrid, Monaco, Hungary-like): processional + VSC pit lottery; pack-damage sticky; climber narratives are SC-timed only.
- **Long-straight street** (Baku, Singapore, Jeddah): do **not** copy Madrid’s zero-overtake prior. Baku historically has real passing on the main straight **and** a high genuine SC rate (walls, debris). Use higher SC/red mass than Madrid, and allow more on-track reordering than Plackett–Luce-from-grid.
- **Hot + heavy braking**: extra brake/cooling/PU DNF, especially rebuilt cars and weak-cooling teams.
- Next is Baku: upgrades mentioned for Williams; Aston weight-saving; triple-header starts. Lawson/Tsunoda/Hadjar status TBD. ANT lead now 81 pts.

## Calibration targets
Headline win/podium were good. Spend effort on (1) front-runner DNF heterogeneity, (2) VSC-vs-SC-vs-red mixture, (3) fatter incident tails for pack starters on processional tracks, (4) compound–timing interaction. Do not retune midfield means that were already within ~1 place.

# 2026 Azerbaijan Grand Prix (Baku) — pre-race forecast

Round 15, Saturday 26 September 2026, 51 laps of the 6.003 km Baku City Circuit.
Weekend brought forward one day for Azerbaijan’s Day of Remembrance. Forecast is after qualifying and grid penalties, before the race.

## Grid (after penalties)

1 Russell (Mercedes) 1:42.526  
2 Leclerc (Ferrari) +0.837

Hadjar returns after missing NED/ITA/ESP with a wrist injury. Lawson is back at Racing Bulls.

## Championship (after Madrid)

Antonelli 292, Russell 211 (−81), Hamilton 191, Norris 186, Leclerc 167, Verstappen 145, Piastri 120. Mercedes 503 in constructors. Antonelli has eight wins; Russell two.

## Pace picture

Mercedes dominated Thursday (Russell FP1/FP2). Verstappen nicked FP3 by 0.099s. Qualifying then split: Russell produced a 0.837s pole — biggest 2026 Mercedes one-lap win — while Antonelli clipped the T1 inside wall in Q1.

F1-compiled long runs tell a different story than that pole lap:

| Team | Est. race gap |
| Mercedes | — |
| McLaren | +0.05s |
| Red Bull | +0.30s |
| Ferrari | +0.34s |
| Alpine | +0.99s |

Russell’s own Thursday comment was that race pace looked closely matched with McLaren and Red Bull. Leclerc’s P2 used tows; Ferrari still trails on the straight. Verstappen was down on power throughout qualifying (~0.5s to Hadjar, 11 km/h down the trap) plus a battery abort and Norris’s yellow. Hadjar’s P4 is genuine but he was cautious on a sore wrist and worried about Red Bull launches into a long T1.

## Race character

Dry, ~26°C air, track ~43°C, 0% rain. Wind calmer than Friday’s 65 km/h quali gusts (race gusts ~43 km/h). Pirelli C3 hard / C4 medium / C5 soft; one-stop favoured, all three compounds live, hard may be ignored. Pit windows wide. 2026 active aero and energy deployment should help passing on the 2.2 km straight relative to older Baku, but the castle section remains a wall.

Unlike Madrid, this is not a processional prior. Baku combines real main-straight passing with a high genuine SC rate (Pirelli’s historical SC figure here is very high; model uses ~76% at least one SC/red rather than 89%, to avoid Madrid-style overfit).

## Model

280k-race Monte Carlo:

- Grid after penalties, with Red Bull start losses (Hadjar, Verstappen) and a T1 pack-damage draw.
- Three interruption regimes: green (~24%), single SC/VSC pit lottery (~44%), multi-SC/red (~32%).
- 68% chance Verstappen’s power is restored overnight.
- Driver-specific mechanical and wall hazards. Extra DNS/mechanical DNF for Antonelli (FP1 hydraulic + fire-damaged PU change + Q1 crash rebuild) following the Madrid Hamilton miss. Elevated Aston–Honda and Cadillac DNF priors held.
- Most retirements are NC; a minority of late stoppages still classify.

Expected classified finishers ≈ 18.2 of 22. P1–P10 almost always filled; P22 occupancy ~1.6%.

## Grid vs call

Material departures: Piastri and Norris over Leclerc (McLaren race pace vs Ferrari, 0.001s quali gap between PIA and LEC); Norris and Hamilton over Hadjar (Red Bull launches + rust); Verstappen over Gasly (true pace, if the PU is even partly healthy); Antonelli from 16th to ~8th (Mercedes delta on a passing straight, SC-dependent for more). Track position holds from Gasly/Colapinto through the Williams/Audi/Cadillac/Aston group, with only small Haas/Racing Bulls swaps.

Antonelli himself said this is harder to overtake than Monza. The call is a points-to-P6 recovery if the car lasts, not a 19th-to-first repeat.

## Madrid (Rd 14) result vs forecast — what to keep vs discard

Result: ANT, VER, NOR, LEC, RUS, LAW, COL, PIA, LIN, HUL | OCO, GAS, BOR, TSU, ALB, BEA, ALO, BOT. NC: HAM (brakes, lap 6), STR (brakes after damage, lap 12), PER (water/PU, lap 31), SAI (collision damage, lap 43). 18 classified vs E≈18.6.

Keep: ANT 36.5% win / NOR 33.9% was the right coin-flip (market +125/+130). Win Brier 0.024, podium Brier 0.026. Midfield almost grid-locked (P9–P18 moved 0 to +2). Processional prior was correct. Stroll highest DNF (~32%) hit. Cadillac/Aston at the back hit. One-stop + hard-to-pass character hit.

Do not overfit: VSC stealing Norris’s win; HAM’s first DNF of the year; Piastri’s T1 wing; F3’s 19 red flags (F1 had one VSC, no SC, no red). Do not bump ANT’s base rate just because he won; do not treat pole as a curse.

## Reusable modeling lessons

### 1. Three interruption regimes, not two
Madrid model mixed (a) green Plackett–Luce and (b) multi-SC/red-flag chaos. The race was a third, more common, modern-F1 state: **a single VSC that is a pit-phase lottery without enabling on-track reordering**.

- Leader who has just passed pit entry cannot stop; P2/P3 can take a cheap stop and jump them. That decided ANT vs NOR. VER also boxed under VSC → P2.
- Cars that park in a runoff gap (Stroll) often produce a **VSC, not a full SC**. Support-series red-flag counts overstate F1 red-flag/SC probability on a new circuit.
- On a no-overtake track, one VSC is enough to decide the win and still leave the rest of the field processional. Chaos-regime mass that lets “best race car from P6” win needs a full SC/red, which did not occur (RUS stayed P5).

Action: add an explicit **single-neutralization pit-lottery** regime. On processional tracks, shave leader win probability toward P2 whenever pit loss is large. Do not let F2/F3 red-flag counts dominate F1 SC/red priors.

### 2. Starting compound × interruption timing is first-order
Early VSC helped cars that **wanted** to stop soon (medium/soft one-stop: ANT, VER, HUL, COL). It hurt hard-tyre long-stint cars (LEC, RUS, PIA, LAW, GAS, BOR) who needed a *late* SC/red.

- LEC led ~32 laps on hards waiting for a late SC/red; pitted lap 48 → P4 (would have been P4 on the other strategy too).
- RUS: hard start, VSC onto mediums, second stop to hard → still P5. Overtaking dead, strategy could not pass LEC.
- GAS/BOR hung out to the end; no late incident → out of points.

Action: do not give generic “climber” points mass from P12–P16 on a processional track unless an interruption is likely *and* timed for their compound. Split-strategy value is timing-dependent, not a free “chaos overlay”.

### 3. Overnight rebuilds and thermal street-circuit DNFs
HAM: FP3 wall at T22, rebuilt overnight, Q4, superb launch, then brake-pedal failure (first DNF of his season). Forecast used a generic ~11% front-runner retirement — same as NOR/VER — and paid for it in retirement/points Brier.

STR also brakes (after early damage) in heat. Bottas spent the race managing brake temps. PER water-pressure/PU. Track into the 50s °C, heavy braking, long straights, banking.

Action:
- After an FP crash/rebuild, bump **mechanical** DNF (brakes, cooling, hydraulics, floor), not only DNS. The car that starts is not a healthy car.
- On hot, heavy-braking street circuits, elevate **brake/cooling/PU thermal** DNF vs “wall hit” DNF. Driver “car killer” quotes overstated *full-course* chaos; they were closer to right on *component* stress.
- Do not apply a uniform ~10–12% DNF to every top-10 car. Rebuild, new PU, and thermal-street flags should differentiate.

Field DNF count was fine (4 vs ~3.4). The miss was **who** DNFed (a P4 Ferrari), not the total.

### 4. Pack-start damage is sticky when passing is dead
Processional Plackett–Luce perturbs order; it understates “broken wing/floor on lap 1 → finish several places down with almost no recovery”.

- PIA: P7, squeezed by RUS, broken endplate, only stop couldn’t fix it, P8. Biggest position log-loss. P(top 10) was fine; the **place distribution was too peaked** around P5–P7.
- TSU: Sainz T1 contact, damaged, P14.
- SAI: T1 lockup vs TSU, later hit ALO, retired with damage.
- STR: opening-lap damage then brakes.

Action: on no-overtake layouts, give P6–P12 a fatter left tail (damage → +3–6 places lost, or NC). Pit-lane starters (BEA) also have little climb without a full SC; P16 from PL is typical, not a points tail.

### 5. Grid still dominates the midfield on this circuit type
COL 9→7, LIN 10→9, HUL 11→10, OCO 13→11, GAS 14→12, BOR 12→13, TSU 15→14, ALB 16→15, ALO 17→17, BOT 19→18. HAM’s early DNF was the main +1 shuffle.

Keep a strong track-position model from ~P8 back. Alpine (Mercedes PU) and Racing Bulls are the real midfield; Audi/Haas next; Williams off the pace; Aston/Cadillac fighting not to be last. Q3 slots (COL, LIN) converting to points is the default if they finish.

GAS as “most likely climber from P14” was the main midfield over-credit. Without a late SC, P14 on a processional track stays ~P12–P14.

### 6. Quali gap of 0.01s: prefer the better race car / championship leader
ANT from P2 beat polesitter after a VSC, but also had genuine Mercedes race pace and FP lockout. NOR was fastest in the race until the VSC; both belong in the high-30s win range when the gap is 0.011s. Do not collapse them to 50/50 on pole alone, and do not treat the VSC outcome as evidence NOR was mis-ranked.

VER P3 is sticky on a processional track if he finishes (here P2 via VSC + HAM DNF). He still could not match ANT/NOR on pace — “best of the rest” remains the Red Bull base.

### 7. Friday compound reading vs Sunday
Pirelli: C2 hard was little-run on Friday and was the race tyre (stints >45 laps). Medium/soft grained but were usable. Teams that over-indexed Friday long runs, or assumed two-stop from graining, were wrong.

Action: on a new street circuit, treat Friday tyre conclusions as weak. High pit loss + no passing makes one-stop the default even if Friday said otherwise. Hard can be the race tyre without Friday evidence.

### 8. Constructor reliability priors (do not shrink yet)
- Aston–Honda: still DNF-prone (STR) and slow (ALO P17). High retirement, near-zero points until the package actually scores.
- Cadillac–Ferrari PU: PER water/PU DNF, BOT last classified, 0 points in 14 races. Keep high DNF, negligible points.
- Williams: no pace (ALB “best we could hope”: beat Astons + one Haas). Points only via chaos.
- Audi: HUL P10 via VSC pit-stop vs OCO. Midfield points are a pit-execution / compound-timing thing, not race-pace overtake.

## Circuit-type flags for later rounds

- **No-overtake street / short T1 run** (Madrid, Monaco, Hungary-like): processional + VSC pit lottery; pack-damage sticky; climber narratives are SC-timed only.
- **Long-straight street** (Baku, Singapore, Jeddah): do **not** copy Madrid’s zero-overtake prior. Baku historically has real passing on the main straight **and** a high genuine SC rate (walls, debris). Use higher SC/red mass than Madrid, and allow more on-track reordering than Plackett–Luce-from-grid.
- **Hot + heavy braking**: extra brake/cooling/PU DNF, especially rebuilt cars and weak-cooling teams.
- Next is Baku: upgrades mentioned for Williams; Aston weight-saving; triple-header starts. Lawson/Tsunoda/Hadjar status TBD. ANT lead now 81 pts.

## Calibration targets
Headline win/podium were good. Spend effort on (1) front-runner DNF heterogeneity, (2) VSC-vs-SC-vs-red mixture, (3) fatter incident tails for pack starters on processional tracks, (4) compound–timing interaction. Do not retune midfield means that were already within ~1 place.

# 2026 Spanish Grand Prix (Madring) — pre-race forecast

Round 14 of the 2026 world championship, Sunday 13 September, 57 laps of the new 5.414 km IFEMA Madrid circuit. Forecast is after qualifying and grid penalties, before the race.

## Grid (after penalties)

1 Norris (McLaren) 1:31.824  
2 Antonelli (Mercedes) +0.011  
3 Verstappen (Red Bull) +0.140  
4 Hamilton (Ferrari) +0.189  
5 Leclerc (Ferrari) +0.195  
6 Russell (Mercedes) +0.325  
7 Piastri (McLaren) +0.470  
8 Lawson (Red Bull) +0.492  
9 Colapinto (Alpine) +1.079  
10 Lindblad (Racing Bulls) +1.217  
11 Hulkenberg (Audi)  
12 Bortoleto (Audi)  
13 Ocon (Haas)  
14 Gasly (Alpine)  
15 Tsunoda (Racing Bulls)  
16 Albon (Williams)  
17 Alonso (Aston Martin)  
18 Perez (Cadillac)  
19 Bottas (Cadillac)  
20 Sainz (Williams, 3-place penalty for impeding Bottas)  
21 Bearman (Haas, no Q time after FP3 crash)  
22 Stroll (Aston Martin, 40-place PU penalty; no Q time)

Hadjar sits out a third race with a wrist injury; Lawson remains in the Red Bull, Tsunoda in the Racing Bulls.

## Championship and form

After 13 races (Monza): Antonelli 267, Russell 201, Hamilton 191, Norris 171, Leclerc 155, Verstappen 127, Piastri 116. Mercedes 468–346 over Ferrari in constructors.

Antonelli has seven wins including a 19th-to-first recovery at Monza last weekend. Mercedes swept practice here (Russell FP1, Antonelli FP2/FP3). Norris has won two of the last three Grands Prix (Hungary, Zandvoort) and produced what he called one of his best laps for pole. Ferrari have been Mercedes’ closest match on Friday/Saturday long-run and one-lap pace. Red Bull are a step behind the top three teams; Verstappen still extracted P3. Alpine (Mercedes PU) and Racing Bulls occupy the real midfield; Audi/Haas next; Williams off the pace; Aston Martin’s Honda package has been a reliability and speed disaster; Cadillac (Ferrari customer PU) has 0 points in 13 races.

## Circuit and race character

Madring is a first-time hybrid street/permanent layout: 22 corners, ~340 km/h on the straights, 24% banked “La Monumental”. F3 testing produced 19 red flags. Verstappen and Williams called it a potential “car killer”. Drivers (Antonelli, Russell, Hamilton, Alpine) all said on-track passing is painful — Antonelli spent two practice laps stuck behind a Williams. The run to Turn 1 is only ~200 m, so the start is bunched rather than a long drag.

Weather: dry, air high-20s/low-30s °C, track into the 50s. No rain. Pirelli C2/C3/C4; one-stop medium–hard is the natural call because pit loss plus hard passing punish an extra stop, though Friday graining and a two-stop (M–H–H) remain live. Norris/Antonelli/Verstappen/Russell/Piastri have no new softs; Hamilton and Leclerc kept a fresh C4 as a start/undercut wildcard. Safety-car market was heavily “yes” (~73%).

## Model

120k-race Monte Carlo with:

- Qualifying grid after penalties, plus a small T1 launch mix (Ferrari’s new-soft option, Verstappen’s starts, short run to T1).
- Two finishing-order regimes: a **processional** Plackett–Luce (track position dominates, matching driver feedback) and a **chaos** regime (multiple SCs / red flag / pit lottery) in which Mercedes race pace can still come through, as at Monza.
- Driver-specific mechanical and wall-incident hazards, elevated versus a mature permanent circuit. Extra DNS risk for Bearman (impact-structure rebuild) and Stroll (fresh Honda PU that already leaked water). Small DSQ risk, slightly higher at the front because of plank/skid wear on the banking.
- 90% rule: most DNFs are NC; a minority of late stoppages still classify.

Win probabilities are close to the post-quali market (Antonelli ≈ Norris, then Verstappen, then the Ferraris) but give Russell more win chance than the +2200 board, because the W17 is still the best race car and one SC cycle is enough to use it.

## Headline probabilities

| Driver | P(win) | P(podium) | P(top 10) | P(retirement) |
|--------|--------|-----------|-----------|----------------|
| Antonelli | 36.5% | 79.5% | 89.0% | 10.0% |
| Norris | 33.9% | 74.1% | 87.3% | 11.8% |
| Verstappen | 10.5% | 52.4% | 87.8% | 11.3% |
| Hamilton | 6.6% | 35.9% | 87.7% | 11.1% |
| Russell | 5.7% | 25.1% | 88.4% | 10.7% |
| Leclerc | 4.1% | 21.0% | 86.2% | 12.8% |
| Piastri | 1.9% | 8.7% | 87.2% | 11.9% |
| Lawson | 0.35% | 1.5% | 81.7% | 15.6% |

Norris vs Antonelli is a coin-flip with a slight edge to the championship leader: pole and dirty-air defence versus the faster Mercedes and a 0.011s qualifying gap. Verstappen’s P3 is sticky if the race stays green; Hamilton/Russell are the cars most likely to break that order under SC. From P8 back, the race is a midfield points fight (Colapinto/Lindblad defending Q3 slots, Gasly the most likely climber from P14, Hulkenberg in the mix). Cadillac and Aston Martin are fighting not to finish last; Stroll’s combination of PU roulette, P22 and 2026 DNF rate is the highest retirement on the grid (~32%).

Expected classified finishers ≈ 18.6 of 22. P1–P11 are essentially always filled; P22 occupancy is only ~2.7% because DNS/NC/DSQ remove cars.

# Forecast notes

## 2026 snapshot (through Rd 14 Madrid)

Drivers: ANT 292, RUS 211, HAM 191, NOR 186, LEC 167, VER 145, PIA 120.
Constructors: Mercedes 503, Ferrari 358, McLaren 306, Red Bull 230, Racing Bulls 77, Alpine 68.
Winners: ANT x8 (CHN, JPN, MIA, CAN, MON, BEL, ITA from P19, ESP), RUS x2, NOR x2, HAM (BCN), LEC (GBR).
Line-up: Hadjar (RB) still out wrist — Lawson in RB, Tsunoda in Racing Bulls (NED/ITA/ESP). Cadillac 0 pts. Aston Honda still a reliability/speed disaster. Next: Baku (Rd 15).

## Madrid (Rd 14) result vs forecast — what to keep vs discard

Result: ANT, VER, NOR, LEC, RUS, LAW, COL, PIA, LIN, HUL | OCO, GAS, BOR, TSU, ALB, BEA, ALO, BOT. NC: HAM (brakes, lap 6), STR (brakes after damage, lap 12), PER (water/PU, lap 31), SAI (collision damage, lap 43). 18 classified vs E≈18.6.

Keep: ANT 36.5% win / NOR 33.9% was the right coin-flip (market +125/+130). Win Brier 0.024, podium Brier 0.026. Midfield almost grid-locked (P9–P18 moved 0 to +2). Processional prior was correct. Stroll highest DNF (~32%) hit. Cadillac/Aston at the back hit. One-stop + hard-to-pass character hit.

Do not overfit: VSC stealing Norris’s win; HAM’s first DNF of the year; Piastri’s T1 wing; F3’s 19 red flags (F1 had one VSC, no SC, no red). Do not bump ANT’s base rate just because he won; do not treat pole as a curse.

## Reusable modeling lessons

### 1. Three interruption regimes, not two
Madrid model mixed (a) green Plackett–Luce and (b) multi-SC/red-flag chaos. The race was a third, more common, modern-F1 state: **a single VSC that is a pit-phase lottery without enabling on-track reordering**.

- Leader who has just passed pit entry cannot stop; P2/P3 can take a cheap stop and jump them. That decided ANT vs NOR. VER also boxed under VSC → P2.
- Cars that park in a runoff gap (Stroll) often produce a **VSC, not a full SC**. Support-series red-flag counts overstate F1 red-flag/SC probability on a new circuit.
- On a no-overtake track, one VSC is enough to decide the win and still leave the rest of the field processional. Chaos-regime mass that lets “best race car from P6” win needs a full SC/red, which did not occur (RUS stayed P5).

Action: add an explicit **single-neutralization pit-lottery** regime. On processional tracks, shave leader win probability toward P2 whenever pit loss is large. Do not let F2/F3 red-flag counts dominate F1 SC/red priors.

### 2. Starting compound × interruption timing is first-order
Early VSC helped cars that **wanted** to stop soon (medium/soft one-stop: ANT, VER, HUL, COL). It hurt hard-tyre long-stint cars (LEC, RUS, PIA, LAW, GAS, BOR) who needed a *late* SC/red.

- LEC led ~32 laps on hards waiting for a late SC/red; pitted lap 48 → P4 (would have been P4 on the other strategy too).
- RUS: hard start, VSC onto mediums, second stop to hard → still P5. Overtaking dead, strategy could not pass LEC.
- GAS/BOR hung out to the end; no late incident → out of points.

Action: do not give generic “climber” points mass from P12–P16 on a processional track unless an interruption is likely *and* timed for their compound. Split-strategy value is timing-dependent, not a free “chaos overlay”.

### 3. Overnight rebuilds and thermal street-circuit DNFs
HAM: FP3 wall at T22, rebuilt overnight, Q4, superb launch, then brake-pedal failure (first DNF of his season). Forecast used a generic ~11% front-runner retirement — same as NOR/VER — and paid for it in retirement/points Brier.

STR also brakes (after early damage) in heat. Bottas spent the race managing brake temps. PER water-pressure/PU. Track into the 50s °C, heavy braking, long straights, banking.

Action:
- After an FP crash/rebuild, bump **mechanical** DNF (brakes, cooling, hydraulics, floor), not only DNS. The car that starts is not a healthy car.
- On hot, heavy-braking street circuits, elevate **brake/cooling/PU thermal** DNF vs “wall hit” DNF. Driver “car killer” quotes overstated *full-course* chaos; they were closer to right on *component* stress.
- Do not apply a uniform ~10–12% DNF to every top-10 car. Rebuild, new PU, and thermal-street flags should differentiate.

Field DNF count was fine (4 vs ~3.4). The miss was **who** DNFed (a P4 Ferrari), not the total.

### 4. Pack-start damage is sticky when passing is dead
Processional Plackett–Luce perturbs order; it understates “broken wing/floor on lap 1 → finish several places down with almost no recovery”.

- PIA: P7, squeezed by RUS, broken endplate, only stop couldn’t fix it, P8. Biggest position log-loss. P(top 10) was fine; the **place distribution was too peaked** around P5–P7.
- TSU: Sainz T1 contact, damaged, P14.
- SAI: T1 lockup vs TSU, later hit ALO, retired with damage.
- STR: opening-lap damage then brakes.

Action: on no-overtake layouts, give P6–P12 a fatter left tail (damage → +3–6 places lost, or NC). Pit-lane starters (BEA) also have little climb without a full SC; P16 from PL is typical, not a points tail.

### 5. Grid still dominates the midfield on this circuit type
COL 9→7, LIN 10→9, HUL 11→10, OCO 13→11, GAS 14→12, BOR 12→13, TSU 15→14, ALB 16→15, ALO 17→17, BOT 19→18. HAM’s early DNF was the main +1 shuffle.

Keep a strong track-position model from ~P8 back. Alpine (Mercedes PU) and Racing Bulls are the real midfield; Audi/Haas next; Williams off the pace; Aston/Cadillac fighting not to be last. Q3 slots (COL, LIN) converting to points is the default if they finish.

GAS as “most likely climber from P14” was the main midfield over-credit. Without a late SC, P14 on a processional track stays ~P12–P14.

### 6. Quali gap of 0.01s: prefer the better race car / championship leader
ANT from P2 beat polesitter after a VSC, but also had genuine Mercedes race pace and FP lockout. NOR was fastest in the race until the VSC; both belong in the high-30s win range when the gap is 0.011s. Do not collapse them to 50/50 on pole alone, and do not treat the VSC outcome as evidence NOR was mis-ranked.

VER P3 is sticky on a processional track if he finishes (here P2 via VSC + HAM DNF). He still could not match ANT/NOR on pace — “best of the rest” remains the Red Bull base.

### 7. Friday compound reading vs Sunday
Pirelli: C2 hard was little-run on Friday and was the race tyre (stints >45 laps). Medium/soft grained but were usable. Teams that over-indexed Friday long runs, or assumed two-stop from graining, were wrong.

Action: on a new street circuit, treat Friday tyre conclusions as weak. High pit loss + no passing makes one-stop the default even if Friday said otherwise. Hard can be the race tyre without Friday evidence.

### 8. Constructor reliability priors (do not shrink yet)
- Aston–Honda: still DNF-prone (STR) and slow (ALO P17). High retirement, near-zero points until the package actually scores.
- Cadillac–Ferrari PU: PER water/PU DNF, BOT last classified, 0 points in 14 races. Keep high DNF, negligible points.
- Williams: no pace (ALB “best we could hope”: beat Astons + one Haas). Points only via chaos.
- Audi: HUL P10 via VSC pit-stop vs OCO. Midfield points are a pit-execution / compound-timing thing, not race-pace overtake.

## Circuit-type flags for later rounds

- **No-overtake street / short T1 run** (Madrid, Monaco, Hungary-like): processional + VSC pit lottery; pack-damage sticky; climber narratives are SC-timed only.
- **Long-straight street** (Baku, Singapore, Jeddah): do **not** copy Madrid’s zero-overtake prior. Baku historically has real passing on the main straight **and** a high genuine SC rate (walls, debris). Use higher SC/red mass than Madrid, and allow more on-track reordering than Plackett–Luce-from-grid.
- **Hot + heavy braking**: extra brake/cooling/PU DNF, especially rebuilt cars and weak-cooling teams.
- Next is Baku: upgrades mentioned for Williams; Aston weight-saving; triple-header starts. Lawson/Tsunoda/Hadjar status TBD. ANT lead now 81 pts.

## Calibration targets
Headline win/podium were good. Spend effort on (1) front-runner DNF heterogeneity, (2) VSC-vs-SC-vs-red mixture, (3) fatter incident tails for pack starters on processional tracks, (4) compound–timing interaction. Do not retune midfield means that were already within ~1 place.

Round 14 of the 2026 world championship, Sunday 13 September, 57 laps of the new 5.414 km IFEMA Madrid circuit. Forecast is after qualifying and grid penalties, before the race.

## Championship and form

After 13 races (Monza): Antonelli 267, Russell 201, Hamilton 191, Norris 171, Leclerc 155, Verstappen 127, Piastri 116. Mercedes 468–346 over Ferrari in constructors.

Antonelli has seven wins including a 19th-to-first recovery at Monza last weekend. Mercedes swept practice here (Russell FP1, Antonelli FP2/FP3). Norris has won two of the last three Grands Prix (Hungary, Zandvoort) and produced what he called one of his best laps for pole. Ferrari have been Mercedes’ closest match on Friday/Saturday long-run and one-lap pace. Red Bull are a step behind the top three teams; Verstappen still extracted P3. Alpine (Mercedes PU) and Racing Bulls occupy the real midfield; Audi/Haas next; Williams off the pace; Aston Martin’s Honda package has been a reliability and speed disaster; Cadillac (Ferrari customer PU) has 0 points in 13 races.

## Circuit and race character

Madring is a first-time hybrid street/permanent layout: 22 corners, ~340 km/h on the straights, 24% banked “La Monumental”. F3 testing produced 19 red flags. Verstappen and Williams called it a potential “car killer”. Drivers (Antonelli, Russell, Hamilton, Alpine) all said on-track passing is painful — Antonelli spent two practice laps stuck behind a Williams. The run to Turn 1 is only ~200 m, so the start is bunched rather than a long drag.

Weather: dry, air high-20s/low-30s °C, track into the 50s. No rain. Pirelli C2/C3/C4; one-stop medium–hard is the natural call because pit loss plus hard passing punish an extra stop, though Friday graining and a two-stop (M–H–H) remain live. Norris/Antonelli/Verstappen/Russell/Piastri have no new softs; Hamilton and Leclerc kept a fresh C4 as a start/undercut wildcard. Safety-car market was heavily “yes” (~73%).

120k-race Monte Carlo with:

- Qualifying grid after penalties, plus a small T1 launch mix (Ferrari’s new-soft option, Verstappen’s starts, short run to T1).
- Two finishing-order regimes: a **processional** Plackett–Luce (track position dominates, matching driver feedback) and a **chaos** regime (multiple SCs / red flag / pit lottery) in which Mercedes race pace can still come through, as at Monza.
- Driver-specific mechanical and wall-incident hazards, elevated versus a mature permanent circuit. Extra DNS risk for Bearman (impact-structure rebuild) and Stroll (fresh Honda PU that already leaked water). Small DSQ risk, slightly higher at the front because of plank/skid wear on the banking.
- 90% rule: most DNFs are NC; a minority of late stoppages still classify.

Win probabilities are close to the post-quali market (Antonelli ≈ Norris, then Verstappen, then the Ferraris) but give Russell more win chance than the +2200 board, because the W17 is still the best race car and one SC cycle is enough to use it.

Result: ANT, VER, NOR, LEC, RUS, LAW, COL, PIA, LIN, HUL | OCO, GAS, BOR, TSU, ALB, BEA, ALO, BOT. NC: HAM (brakes, lap 6), STR (brakes after damage, lap 12), PER (water/PU, lap 31), SAI (collision damage, lap 43). 18 classified vs E≈18.6.

## Reusable modeling lessons

### 1. Three interruption regimes, not two
Madrid model mixed (a) green Plackett–Luce and (b) multi-SC/red-flag chaos. The race was a third, more common, modern-F1 state: **a single VSC that is a pit-phase lottery without enabling on-track reordering**.

- Leader who has just passed pit entry cannot stop; P2/P3 can take a cheap stop and jump them. That decided ANT vs NOR. VER also boxed under VSC → P2.
- Cars that park in a runoff gap (Stroll) often produce a **VSC, not a full SC**. Support-series red-flag counts overstate F1 red-flag/SC probability on a new circuit.
- On a no-overtake track, one VSC is enough to decide the win and still leave the rest of the field processional. Chaos-regime mass that lets “best race car from P6” win needs a full SC/red, which did not occur (RUS stayed P5).

Action: add an explicit **single-neutralization pit-lottery** regime. On processional tracks, shave leader win probability toward P2 whenever pit loss is large. Do not let F2/F3 red-flag counts dominate F1 SC/red priors.

### 2. Starting compound × interruption timing is first-order
Early VSC helped cars that **wanted** to stop soon (medium/soft one-stop: ANT, VER, HUL, COL). It hurt hard-tyre long-stint cars (LEC, RUS, PIA, LAW, GAS, BOR) who needed a *late* SC/red.

- LEC led ~32 laps on hards waiting for a late SC/red; pitted lap 48 → P4 (would have been P4 on the other strategy too).
- RUS: hard start, VSC onto mediums, second stop to hard → still P5. Overtaking dead, strategy could not pass LEC.
- GAS/BOR hung out to the end; no late incident → out of points.

Action: do not give generic “climber” points mass from P12–P16 on a processional track unless an interruption is likely *and* timed for their compound. Split-strategy value is timing-dependent, not a free “chaos overlay”.

### 3. Overnight rebuilds and thermal street-circuit DNFs
HAM: FP3 wall at T22, rebuilt overnight, Q4, superb launch, then brake-pedal failure (first DNF of his season). Forecast used a generic ~11% front-runner retirement — same as NOR/VER — and paid for it in retirement/points Brier.

STR also brakes (after early damage) in heat. Bottas spent the race managing brake temps. PER water-pressure/PU. Track into the 50s °C, heavy braking, long straights, banking.

Action:
- After an FP crash/rebuild, bump **mechanical** DNF (brakes, cooling, hydraulics, floor), not only DNS. The car that starts is not a healthy car.
- On hot, heavy-braking street circuits, elevate **brake/cooling/PU thermal** DNF vs “wall hit” DNF. Driver “car killer” quotes overstated *full-course* chaos; they were closer to right on *component* stress.
- Do not apply a uniform ~10–12% DNF to every top-10 car. Rebuild, new PU, and thermal-street flags should differentiate.

Field DNF count was fine (4 vs ~3.4). The miss was **who** DNFed (a P4 Ferrari), not the total.

### 4. Pack-start damage is sticky when passing is dead
Processional Plackett–Luce perturbs order; it understates “broken wing/floor on lap 1 → finish several places down with almost no recovery”.

- PIA: P7, squeezed by RUS, broken endplate, only stop couldn’t fix it, P8. Biggest position log-loss. P(top 10) was fine; the **place distribution was too peaked** around P5–P7.
- TSU: Sainz T1 contact, damaged, P14.
- SAI: T1 lockup vs TSU, later hit ALO, retired with damage.
- STR: opening-lap damage then brakes.

Action: on no-overtake layouts, give P6–P12 a fatter left tail (damage → +3–6 places lost, or NC). Pit-lane starters (BEA) also have little climb without a full SC; P16 from PL is typical, not a points tail.

### 5. Grid still dominates the midfield on this circuit type
COL 9→7, LIN 10→9, HUL 11→10, OCO 13→11, GAS 14→12, BOR 12→13, TSU 15→14, ALB 16→15, ALO 17→17, BOT 19→18. HAM’s early DNF was the main +1 shuffle.

Keep a strong track-position model from ~P8 back. Alpine (Mercedes PU) and Racing Bulls are the real midfield; Audi/Haas next; Williams off the pace; Aston/Cadillac fighting not to be last. Q3 slots (COL, LIN) converting to points is the default if they finish.

GAS as “most likely climber from P14” was the main midfield over-credit. Without a late SC, P14 on a processional track stays ~P12–P14.

### 6. Quali gap of 0.01s: prefer the better race car / championship leader
ANT from P2 beat polesitter after a VSC, but also had genuine Mercedes race pace and FP lockout. NOR was fastest in the race until the VSC; both belong in the high-30s win range when the gap is 0.011s. Do not collapse them to 50/50 on pole alone, and do not treat the VSC outcome as evidence NOR was mis-ranked.

VER P3 is sticky on a processional track if he finishes (here P2 via VSC + HAM DNF). He still could not match ANT/NOR on pace — “best of the rest” remains the Red Bull base.

### 7. Friday compound reading vs Sunday
Pirelli: C2 hard was little-run on Friday and was the race tyre (stints >45 laps). Medium/soft grained but were usable. Teams that over-indexed Friday long runs, or assumed two-stop from graining, were wrong.

Action: on a new street circuit, treat Friday tyre conclusions as weak. High pit loss + no passing makes one-stop the default even if Friday said otherwise. Hard can be the race tyre without Friday evidence.

### 8. Constructor reliability priors (do not shrink yet)
- Aston–Honda: still DNF-prone (STR) and slow (ALO P17). High retirement, near-zero points until the package actually scores.
- Cadillac–Ferrari PU: PER water/PU DNF, BOT last classified, 0 points in 14 races. Keep high DNF, negligible points.
- Williams: no pace (ALB “best we could hope”: beat Astons + one Haas). Points only via chaos.
- Audi: HUL P10 via VSC pit-stop vs OCO. Midfield points are a pit-execution / compound-timing thing, not race-pace overtake.

## Circuit-type flags for later rounds

- **No-overtake street / short T1 run** (Madrid, Monaco, Hungary-like): processional + VSC pit lottery; pack-damage sticky; climber narratives are SC-timed only.
- **Long-straight street** (Baku, Singapore, Jeddah): do **not** copy Madrid’s zero-overtake prior. Baku historically has real passing on the main straight **and** a high genuine SC rate (walls, debris). Use higher SC/red mass than Madrid, and allow more on-track reordering than Plackett–Luce-from-grid.
- **Hot + heavy braking**: extra brake/cooling/PU DNF, especially rebuilt cars and weak-cooling teams.
- Next is Baku: upgrades mentioned for Williams; Aston weight-saving; triple-header starts. Lawson/Tsunoda/Hadjar status TBD. ANT lead now 81 pts.

## Calibration targets
Headline win/podium were good. Spend effort on (1) front-runner DNF heterogeneity, (2) VSC-vs-SC-vs-red mixture, (3) fatter incident tails for pack starters on processional tracks, (4) compound–timing interaction. Do not retune midfield means that were already within ~1 place.

TITLE: 2026 Azerbaijan Grand Prix race report and highlights: George Russell narrowly holds off Max Verstappen to take victory over the line in chaotic Azerbaijan Grand Prix
 2026 Azerbaijan Grand Prix race report and highlights: George Russell narrowly holds off Max Verstappen to take victory over the line in chaotic Azerbaijan Grand Prix Skip to content Race Series Authentics (opens in a new tab) Store (opens in a new tab) Tickets (opens in a new tab) Hospitality (opens in a new tab) Experiences (opens in a new tab) Arcade (opens in a new tab) F1 TV (opens in a new tab) Sign In Subscribe F1 Schedule Results Standings Drivers Teams F1 Unlocked Open menu FIA Azerbaijan Race 2026 Russell narrowly holds off Verstappen to take victory over the line in chaotic Azerbaijan GP George Russell avoided multiple incidents to pip Max Verstappen to the win in Baku. Sep 26, 2026 12:54pm UTC George Russell survived a late challenge from Max Verstappen to secure his third victory of the season in a dramatic Azerbaijan Grand Prix that saw six drivers retire, including McLaren’s Lando Norris. The Mercedes driver built on a strong start to control the first half, leaving Oscar Piastri to defend against the charging Red Bull pair of Verstappen and Isack Hadjar while Russell extended his lead. An error from Williams’ Alex Albon shook up the race as the Safety Car was deployed and the Briton battled to hold on at the restart, but the action was halted for a second time when Franco Colapinto locked up, taking out his Alpine team mate Pierre Gasly and Norris. With the field neutralised again, Russell came under immense pressure from Verstappen on the final laps and ultimately crossed the line just one tenth ahead, denying the Dutchman what could’ve been his first win of the season. Isack Hadjar was third to clinch a double podium for Red Bull, with Charles Leclerc and Kimi Antonelli taking P4 and P5 – the Italian made the most of the chaos in front to improve from P16 to the points. Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton was a lonely sixth ahead of Arvid Lindblad, who beat Esteban Ocon to P7 over the line, Ollie Bearman and Carlos Sainz as Haas celebrated scoring for the first time since the Monaco Grand Prix. Race results FORMULA 1 QATAR AIRWAYS AZERBAIJAN GRAND PRIX 2026 Pos. Driver Time Points 1 George Russell RUS 1:38:02.143 25 2 Max Verstappen VER +0.196s 18 3 Isack Hadjar HAD +10.704s 15 4 Charles Leclerc LEC +14.136s 12 5 Kimi Antonelli ANT +14.512s 10 View all standings Audi’s Nico Hulkenberg placed P11 after losing out to the lead Williams with two laps to go while Liam Lawson settled for P12, the New Zealander left frustrated following contact with his Racing Bulls team mate. With P13 belonging to Gabriel Bortoleto, Oscar Piastri wound up P14 despite running in the podium positions for the majority of the race. A lock-up dropped him outside of the points and he led Cadillac’s Sergio Perez as the last of the finishers. Valtteri Bottas drove into the barriers late on and was the final driver to DNF, joining Albon, Colapinto, Norris and Pierre Gasly. The Aston Martin duo of Fernando Alonso and Lance Stroll also failed to finish due to separate mechanical issues. AS IT HAPPENED The tricky Baku City Circuit had already caught out plenty of drivers over the weekend, and even championship leader Antonelli – who had largely been faultless this season – wasn’t immune to the track’s challenges. He hit the wall at Turn 1 in the opening segment of Qualifying, resulting in damage that ruled him out of the rest of the session. As a result, the Italian was set to line up in P16, significantly adrift of his dominant Mercedes team mate. Russell had delivered a superlative lap in Q3 to secure pole position by the biggest margin of the year – 0.837s over Ferrari’s Leclerc. It gave him the confidence to target his first victory since Round 8 in Austria, but as previous races in Baku have shown, anything could happen. Those behind Russell were remarkably close in Qualifying, with Piastri – eager for redemption after crashing out of this event in 2025 – and Hadjar lining up alongside one another on the second row, followed by Norris and Hamilton. There had been some alterations to the order prior to the start, with Williams’ Sainz demoted from P9 to P14 due to a yellow flag infringement. Perez was also penalised after he impeded Piastri, though his position of P20 remained unchanged, while both Aston Martin drivers received grid penalties for the use of additional power unit elements, relegating them to the back row. Antonelli had work to do after he crashed out of Qualifying As the field took to their grid spots, it was revealed that there was an almost equal split between medium and soft tyres on display, with Russell, Norris, Gasly, Verstappen and Colapinto those in the top 10 to opt for the former. Leclerc, Piastri, Hadjar, Hamilton, Bearman and the trio on the outskirts of the points had gone for the more aggressive strategy of starting on the red-walled compound, likely with the aim of making up places in the early laps. They were joined by Alonso and Stroll at the back, while everyone else – including the out-of-position Antonelli – bolted on the mediums. After a clean formation lap, the five lights went out and Russell enjoyed a great launch as Piastri improved to P2, leaving Leclerc in the clutches of the second McLaren of Norris who had surged past Hadjar for P4. Verstappen also gained spots from Gasly and Hamilton, carrying out a smart move down the inside to pass the Ferrari, but further back, Antonelli’s mission to move up the order had got off to a nightmare start as he dropped back to P17. Meanwhile, his team mate had already opened up an advantage of 1.2s at the front of the pack and was seemingly under little pressure from Piastri, but the Red Bull pair were on the charge – Hadjar snatched fourth place back from Norris before the Briton lost out to Verstappen soon after. That wasn’t enough for the Frenchman and he went after Leclerc next, sweeping around the outside of Turn 1 in an attempt to displace the Monegasque. Although he couldn’t quite stay ahead, he got the move done a few corners later to take P3. Red Bull’s brilliant first stint continued as Verstappen similarly dispatched Leclerc with ease, prompting Piastri’s race engineer to encourage the Aussie to keep them “out of range”. However, it didn’t take long for Hadjar to get within a second of the McLaren, with his team mate posting the fastest lap of the race almost simultaneously. That meant that it wasn’t a surprise when the Dutchman powered past Hadjar down the main straight following an instruction from the team, and he rapidly closed up to challenge Piastri, who was fighting to cling onto second place whilst reporting concerns with his rear tyres. Elsewhere, Antonelli had overtaken Lindblad, Sainz and Ocon to take P13, but his deficit to Russell was looking more difficult to overhaul with every lap as the Briton eked out a lead of 5s, calmly controlling the race. The first yellow flag of the day was shown on Lap 9 as Aston Martin ordered Stroll to stop with a water pressure issue – the Canadian pulled off in a safe spot, preventing the need for any intervention from race control. Russell established a considerable lead over the rest of the field While Piastri, Verstappen and Hadjar ran within less than 2s of one another, Antonelli patiently waited to capitalise on a similarly close battle between Racing Bulls’ Lawson and Williams’ Albon, which allowed the Italian to eventually pass both and creep closer to the points. There was another change among the frontrunners as Norris locked up and went deep at Turn 5, offering Hamilton the perfect opportunity to set his sights on P6. The narrow section of the track enabled the McLaren driver to stay ahead temporarily, but once it opened back up, Hamilton found a way through. Their short contest demonstrated just how tight the field was as the soft tyre runners entered the pit window, with no one wanting to be the first to head in and subsequently tumble down the order. However, Verstappen was starting to struggle as he reported that his medium tyres were “not good”, leading to an odd exchange within the team – Hadjar questioned the Dutchman’s pace and asked Red Bull to “tell him to keep pushing”, before changing his mind and claiming that his tyres were still performing well. He nevertheless remained behind his team mate, but back at the front, Russell was experiencing his own tyre troubles. Driving nearly 10s ahead of Piastri at the halfway point, he brushed the wall at Turn 15 and asked Mercedes to keep an eye on the pressure, worrying that it “doesn’t feel quite right”. The Red Bull pair raced in tandem around the Baku streets Norris was the next to make an error as he locked up at high speed down the start/finish straight, taking to the run-off area and losing two places to Gasly and Antonelli. But he wasn’t the only one – Albon also suffered a lock-up and drove into the barrier at Turn 6, bringing his race to an early finish. The Safety Car was deployed to recover his abandoned Williams, giving the leaders the chance to peel into the pits and take on fresh rubber that was intended to last them until the end of the Grand Prix. After Red Bull executed an immaculate double stack to keep the order as it was, Hadjar said he was “going to need his help with Piastri” in reference to Verstappen, suggesting that the team were focused on achieving a minimum 2-3 finish with their drivers. That goal was thrown into jeopardy when the Frenchman was warned about vibrations in the gearbox, but he quickly had to switch his attention to the restart. Russell just about held onto the lead as Verstappen finally succeeded in taking P2 away from Piastri, with chaos unfolding further behind. Approaching the Turn 1 braking zone, Colapinto locked up and bumped into his Alpine team mate, who consequently couldn’t avoid hitting McLaren’s Norris. All three went off the track and ultimately retired from the race, resulting in another Safety Car period to clear the debris. There was even more intra-team contact between the Racing Bulls pair as the 19-year-old tagged Lawson’s rear wheel – the New Zealander was understandably not best pleased and sarcastically commented: “I love getting taken out by my team mate. That’s pretty sick.” When the action got underway once again, Russell had more control over the restart and kept the lead Red Bull behind, but disaster struck for Piastri whilst running in third place. Just as others had done earlier on, he locked up at the first turn and had to spin around to rejoin the circuit, which saw him plummet down the order to P15. Amid the chaos, Antonelli had been bumped up to P6 and piled the pressure on Hamilton, with the Italian sailing past down the main straight with eight laps remaining. Verstappen was keen to make a similar pass on the lead Mercedes and consistently fought to stay close enough to force an error. He and Russell were separated by just a few tenths and it increasingly looked like the battle for victory would go down to the wire, with both drivers pushing the limits around the circuit. A yellow flag threatened to disrupt their exhilarating head-to-head when Cadillac’s Bottas found the wall, but they could continue to race as they began the 51st and final lap. Although Verstappen stuck as close by as possible and pulled alongside down the start/finish straight, he couldn’t quite get ahead of Russell and crossed the line 0.1s behind the Mercedes. Russell came under intense pressure from Verstappen on the final laps The thrilling conclusion saw Russell take his eighth career win while Red Bull ended up with a double podium finish, Hadjar securing P3 ahead of Leclerc, Antonelli – who successfully limited the damage of his Qualifying crash – and Hamilton. Lindblad overtook Ocon over the line for P7 as both Haas drivers finished in the top 10 for the first time this season, with Bearman and Sainz the last of the points scorers.  2026 Azerbaijan Grand Prix race report and highlights: George Russell narrowly holds off Max Verstappen to take victory over the line in chaotic Azerbaijan Grand Prix Skip to content Race Series Authentics (opens in a new tab) Store (opens in a new tab) Tickets (opens in a new tab) Hospitality (opens in a new tab) Experiences (opens in a new tab) Arcade (opens in a new tab) F1 TV (opens in a new tab) Sign In Subscribe F1 Schedule Results Standings Drivers Teams F1 Unlocked Open menu FIA Azerbaijan Race 2026 Russell narrowly holds off Verstappen to take victory over the line in chaotic Azerbaijan GP George Russell avoided multiple incidents to pip Max Verstappen to the win in Baku. Sep 26, 2026 12:54pm UTC George Russell survived a late challenge from Max Verstappen to secure his third victory of the season in a dramatic Azerbaijan Grand Prix that saw six drivers retire, including McLaren’s Lando Norris. The Mercedes driver built on a strong start to control the first half, leaving Oscar Piastri to defend against the charging Red Bull pair of Verstappen and Isack Hadjar while Russell extended his lead. An error from Williams’ Alex Albon shook up the race as the Safety Car was deployed and the Briton battled to hold on at the restart, but the action was halted for a second time when Franco Colapinto locked up, taking out his Alpine team mate Pierre Gasly and Norris. With the field neutralised again, Russell came under immense pressure from Verstappen on the final laps and ultimately crossed the line just one tenth ahead, denying the Dutchman what could’ve been his first win of the season. Isack Hadjar was third to clinch a double podium for Red Bull, with Charles Leclerc and Kimi Antonelli taking P4 and P5 – the Italian made the most of the chaos in front to improve from P16 to the points. Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton was a lonely sixth ahead of Arvid Lindblad, who beat Esteban Ocon to P7 over the line, Ollie Bearman and Carlos Sainz as Haas celebrated scoring for the first time since the Monaco Grand Prix. Race results FORMULA 1 QATAR AIRWAYS AZERBAIJAN GRAND PRIX 2026 Pos. Driver Time Points 1 George Russell RUS 1:38:02.143 25 2 Max Verstappen VER +0.196s 18 3 Isack Hadjar HAD +10.704s 15 4 Charles Leclerc LEC +14.136s 12 5 Kimi Antonelli ANT +14.512s 10 View all standings Audi’s Nico Hulkenberg placed P11 after losing out to the lead Williams with two laps to go while Liam Lawson settled for P12, the New Zealander left frustrated following contact with his Racing Bulls team mate. With P13 belonging to Gabriel Bortoleto, Oscar Piastri wound up P14 despite running in the podium positions for the majority of the race. A lock-up dropped him outside of the points and he led Cadillac’s Sergio Perez as the last of the finishers. Valtteri Bottas drove into the barriers late on and was the final driver to DNF, joining Albon, Colapinto, Norris and Pierre Gasly. The Aston Martin duo of Fernando Alonso and Lance Stroll also failed to finish due to separate mechanical issues. AS IT HAPPENED The tricky Baku City Circuit had already caught out plenty of drivers over the weekend, and even championship leader Antonelli – who had largely been faultless this season – wasn’t immune to the track’s challenges. He hit the wall at Turn 1 in the opening segment of Qualifying, resulting in damage that ruled him out of the rest of the session. As a result, the Italian was set to line up in P16, significantly adrift of his dominant Mercedes team mate. Russell had delivered a superlative lap in Q3 to secure pole position by the biggest margin of the year – 0.837s over Ferrari’s Leclerc. It gave him the confidence to target his first victory since Round 8 in Austria, but as previous races in Baku have shown, anything could happen. Those behind Russell were remarkably close in Qualifying, with Piastri – eager for redemption after crashing out of this event in 2025 – and Hadjar lining up alongside one another on the second row, followed by Norris and Hamilton. There had been some alterations to the order prior to the start, with Williams’ Sainz demoted from P9 to P14 due to a yellow flag infringement. Perez was also penalised after he impeded Piastri, though his position of P20 remained unchanged, while both Aston Martin drivers received grid penalties for the use of additional power unit elements, relegating them to the back row. Antonelli had work to do after he crashed out of Qualifying As the field took to their grid spots, it was revealed that there was an almost equal split between medium and soft tyres on display, with Russell, Norris, Gasly, Verstappen and Colapinto those in the top 10 to opt for the former. Leclerc, Piastri, Hadjar, Hamilton, Bearman and the trio on the outskirts of the points had gone for the more aggressive strategy of starting on the red-walled compound, likely with the aim of making up places in the early laps. They were joined by Alonso and Stroll at the back, while everyone else – including the out-of-position Antonelli – bolted on the mediums. After a clean formation lap, the five lights went out and Russell enjoyed a great launch as Piastri improved to P2, leaving Leclerc in the clutches of the second McLaren of Norris who had surged past Hadjar for P4. Verstappen also gained spots from Gasly and Hamilton, carrying out a smart move down the inside to pass the Ferrari, but further back, Antonelli’s mission to move up the order had got off to a nightmare start as he dropped back to P17. Meanwhile, his team mate had already opened up an advantage of 1.2s at the front of the pack and was seemingly under little pressure from Piastri, but the Red Bull pair were on the charge – Hadjar snatched fourth place back from Norris before the Briton lost out to Verstappen soon after. That wasn’t enough for the Frenchman and he went after Leclerc next, sweeping around the outside of Turn 1 in an attempt to displace the Monegasque. Although he couldn’t quite stay ahead, he got the move done a few corners later to take P3. Red Bull’s brilliant first stint continued as Verstappen similarly dispatched Leclerc with ease, prompting Piastri’s race engineer to encourage the Aussie to keep them “out of range”. However, it didn’t take long for Hadjar to get within a second of the McLaren, with his team mate posting the fastest lap of the race almost simultaneously. That meant that it wasn’t a surprise when the Dutchman powered past Hadjar down the main straight following an instruction from the team, and he rapidly closed up to challenge Piastri, who was fighting to cling onto second place whilst reporting concerns with his rear tyres. Elsewhere, Antonelli had overtaken Lindblad, Sainz and Ocon to take P13, but his deficit to Russell was looking more difficult to overhaul with every lap as the Briton eked out a lead of 5s, calmly controlling the race. The first yellow flag of the day was shown on Lap 9 as Aston Martin ordered Stroll to stop with a water pressure issue – the Canadian pulled off in a safe spot, preventing the need for any intervention from race control. Russell established a considerable lead over the rest of the field While Piastri, Verstappen and Hadjar ran within less than 2s of one another, Antonelli patiently waited to capitalise on a similarly close battle between Racing Bulls’ Lawson and Williams’ Albon, which allowed the Italian to eventually pass both and creep closer to the points. There was another change among the frontrunners as Norris locked up and went deep at Turn 5, offering Hamilton the perfect opportunity to set his sights on P6. The narrow section of the track enabled the McLaren driver to stay ahead temporarily, but once it opened back up, Hamilton found a way through. Their short contest demonstrated just how tight the field was as the soft tyre runners entered the pit window, with no one wanting to be the first to head in and subsequently tumble down the order. However, Verstappen was starting to struggle as he reported that his medium tyres were “not good”, leading to an odd exchange within the team – Hadjar questioned the Dutchman’s pace and asked Red Bull to “tell him to keep pushing”, before changing his mind and claiming that his tyres were still performing well. He nevertheless remained behind his team mate, but back at the front, Russell was experiencing his own tyre troubles. Driving nearly 10s ahead of Piastri at the halfway point, he brushed the wall at Turn 15 and asked Mercedes to keep an eye on the pressure, worrying that it “doesn’t feel quite right”. The Red Bull pair raced in tandem around the Baku streets Norris was the next to make an error as he locked up at high speed down the start/finish straight, taking to the run-off area and losing two places to Gasly and Antonelli. But he wasn’t the only one – Albon also suffered a lock-up and drove into the barrier at Turn 6, bringing his race to an early finish. The Safety Car was deployed to recover his abandoned Williams, giving the leaders the chance to peel into the pits and take on fresh rubber that was intended to last them until the end of the Grand Prix. After Red Bull executed an immaculate double stack to keep the order as it was, Hadjar said he was “going to need his help with Piastri” in reference to Verstappen, suggesting that the team were focused on achieving a minimum 2-3 finish with their drivers. That goal was thrown into jeopardy when the Frenchman was warned about vibrations in the gearbox, but he quickly had to switch his attention to the restart. Russell just about held onto the lead as Verstappen finally succeeded in taking P2 away from Piastri, with chaos unfolding further behind. Approaching the Turn 1 braking zone, Colapinto locked up and bumped into his Alpine team mate, who consequently couldn’t avoid hitting McLaren’s Norris. All three went off the track and ultimately retired from the race, resulting in another Safety Car period to clear the debris. There was even more intra-team contact between the Racing Bulls pair as the 19-year-old tagged Lawson’s rear wheel – the New Zealander was understandably not best pleased and sarcastically commented: “I love getting taken out by my team mate. That’s pretty sick.” When the action got underway once again, Russell had more control over the restart and kept the lead Red Bull behind, but disaster struck for Piastri whilst running in third place. Just as others had done earlier on, he locked up at the first turn and had to spin around to rejoin the circuit, which saw him plummet down the order to P15. Amid the chaos, Antonelli had been bumped up to P6 and piled the pressure on Hamilton, with the Italian sailing past down the main straight with eight laps remaining. Verstappen was keen to make a similar pass on the lead Mercedes and consistently fought to stay close enough to force an error. He and Russell were separated by just a few tenths and it increasingly looked like the battle for victory would go down to the wire, with both drivers pushing the limits around the circuit. A yellow flag threatened to disrupt their exhilarating head-to-head when Cadillac’s Bottas found the wall, but they could continue to race as they began the 51st and final lap. Although Verstappen stuck as close by as possible and pulled alongside down the start/finish straight, he couldn’t quite get ahead of Russell and crossed the line 0.1s behind the Mercedes. Russell came under intense pressure from Verstappen on the final laps The thrilling conclusion saw Russell take his eighth career win while Red Bull ended up with a double podium finish, Hadjar securing P3 ahead of Leclerc, Antonelli – who successfully limited the damage of his Qualifying crash – and Hamilton. Lindblad overtook Ocon over the line for P7 as both Haas drivers finished in the top 10 for the first time this season, with Bearman and Sainz the last of the points scorers. The second Safety Car followed a chain of retirements after Colapinto locked up at T1 and hit Gasly, who then struck Norris. Piastri also locked up at T1 on the second restart, dropping from third to fifteenth. Hamilton finished sixth without appearing to pit, which is puzzling given his soft tire start; he may have pitted and the report omitted it.

Hamilton must have pitted during the first Safety Car. He started on soft tires and could not have lasted fifty-one laps without refueling.

Verstappen began from eighth place on medium tires. He gained positions at the start and passed Norris, Leclerc, Hadjar, and Piastri before the second restart. His power unit remained healthy throughout, and he finished only 0.2 seconds behind the winner.

Verstappen finished second, well above the forecast's expected seventh place. The bimodal model averaged a healthy power unit scenario to roughly seventh, but the actual race played out as that higher mode. He passed Gasly and Hamilton at the start, then Norris, Leclerc, and Hadjar before the first pit window, confirming the unit was repaired.

Hadjar started fourth but lost to Norris at the start. He recovered to third place, finishing just behind Verstappen after a team instruction. The forecast had him losing at T1 due to launches and wrist rust, but he was actually excellent. He hit the podium at seventeen point two percent and ranked sixth in predicted order.

The McLaren forecast also misranked the drivers. Piastri was predicted second with a seventeen point six percent win probability and fifty-eight point nine percent podium chance. Norris was predicted third with twelve point one percent and forty-eight point seven percent.

Piastri led second place for most of the race. He lost it to Verstappen at the first Safety Car restart. Then he locked up at T1 on the second restart and dropped from third to fifteenth, finishing fourteenth.

Norris had a T5 lockup and another lockup at the start and finish that cost him two places. He was then caught in the Alpine crash chain and retired on lap thirty-five.

The McLaren forecast wrongly assumed they were hunting Russell. In reality Red Bull were chasing Piastri while Russell pulled away by about ten seconds. This pace miss was the key error.

The long-run data was wrong. Russell opened a 1.2-second gap immediately and held it at roughly 5 seconds while controlling, then pulled to about 10 seconds by halfway. That pace is more than 0.4 seconds per lap, so the compiled long-run read was unreliable. The qualifying gap better reflected the actual race gap.

Leclerc started second but lost to Piastri at the start, then dropped to third behind Hadjar and Verstappen.

Leclerc finished fourth, matching the forecast. The Ferrari race delta was weaker than expected, confirming the front-row did not convert.

Antonelli started sixteenth and climbed to fifth place. The forecast expected around eighth with a twenty-three percent retirement risk, but he finished fifth. The rebuild DNF flag did not trigger; seventy-seven percent of drivers finish, so the Madrid bumping lesson was reasonable yet did not apply this time.

Antonelli said this was the worst weekend of his season, yet he still scored ten points from sixteenth place.

Hamilton finished sixth, one spot below the forecast. He started on soft tires and never challenged for the lead.

The Alpine drivers were both eliminated in the teammate crash. The forecast had them finishing ninth and tenth, which was classic Baku randomness.

Lindblad recovered from fifteenth to seventh place. The forecast had him at fifteenth with a twenty-two percent retirement risk and only two points. He tagged his teammate Lawson in the chaos and finished ahead of Ocon.

Ocon placed eighth and Bearman ninth. Both Haas drivers scored points for the first time since Monaco. The forecast had Bearman eleventh and Ocon thirteenth.

Sainz started fourteenth but received a penalty and finished tenth. The forecast expected him at sixteenth.

Sainz recovered modestly to tenth place, scoring one point. This partially matched the forecast's expectation of a modest recovery rather than a points raid.

Lawson finished twelfth, one spot below the forecast. He was tagged by Lindblad and gained an extra pit lap on lap thirty-six.

Perez finished fifteenth. Bottas retired on lap sixteen after hitting the wall late. The forecast had predicted a high DNF rate for Bottas, but the result was mixed.

Alonso and Stroll both retired from mechanical issues. Stroll lost water pressure while Alonso had a separate mechanical failure. The forecast correctly flagged them as the highest DNF risk.

Alpine had been on course to slash the nine-point gap to Racing Bulls for fifth in the teams' standings , but instead have fallen six points further adrift as Arvid Lindblad finished seventh. The F1 rookie also collided with team mate Liam Lawson at the same time as the Alpines, with that incident ultimately concluding with no further action from the stewards. "I don't think I really have words and I don't need the words now," said Gasly when asked to give his verdict on the incident with Colapinto. "We'll manage it together as a team.
